items.l1_lead: 卡尔·弗里斯顿提出，个体行为与意识、预测和自由意志之间存在复杂关系，强调个体存在与对世界的感知密切相关，为理解人类意识提供新视角。
items.l2_summary:
卡尔·弗里斯顿（Karl Friston）在其研究中探讨了个体行为与存在之间的关系，提出个体的行为可以被视为在为自身存在收集证据。这一观点强调了个体存在与其对世界的感知和解释之间的密切联系，揭示了意识、预测（prediction）、推理（inference）以及个体在生活中所扮演的角色（agency）之间的复杂关系。弗里斯顿的理论暗示，自由意志（free will）和智能（intelligence）在认知（cognition）过程中扮演着重要角色，形成了一种循环性思维模式。

通过这一框架，弗里斯顿为理解人类意识的本质提供了新的视角。他的研究表明，个体在面对环境时，不仅仅是被动反应，而是积极地进行预测和推理，以便更好地适应和生存。这种行为模式不仅涉及到对外部世界的理解，也与个体内在的意识状态密切相关。弗里斯顿的观点挑战了传统对自由意志的理解，强调了个体在认知过程中所拥有的主动性和选择权。

总的来说，弗里斯顿的理论为我们提供了一个新的框架，帮助我们更深入地理解意识的运作机制，以及个体如何在复杂的环境中进行有效的决策和行为。这种对意识、预测和自由意志之间关系的探讨，不仅丰富了我们对人类认知的理解，也为未来的研究指明了方向。

items.title: Escaping The Bunker: Bobby Gillespie On Primal Scream’s Most Uncompromising Era - clashmusic.com
items.body:
原话：“I think people like myself have been in opposition all our lives.” / “We just followed our hearts. We weren’t in competition with any other band.” / “I’m trying to write the newest Primal Scream song.”
论点：他认为Primal Scream的音乐是对当时英国音乐的反叛，强调追随内心而非竞争。

items.article_body:
Bobby Gillespie is a raconteur. A true punk, the Glasgow-born frontman has led Primal Scream through multiple iterations and evolutions, refusing to be hemmed in by expectations. For some fans, their peak came as the debauchery of the 90s collapsed into the paranoia of the Millennium, with a triptych of albums – ‘Vanishing Point’, ‘XTRMNTR’ and ‘Evil Heat’ – presenting the group at their most sonically and politically uncompromising.
Now, he’s taking a rare glimpse back. Spruced up for a lavish re-issue project and an accompanying nationwide tour, ‘The Bunker Trilogy’ – as band mate Andrew Innes terms this period – remains a bracing, inspired listen, a fusion of post-punk, jazz, club culture electronics, and revolutionary politics.
“The idea was: no rules,” he tells CLASH. “Those albums were all recorded in a particular way. We deconstructed the band after ‘Give Out But Don’t Give Up’ – we lost some members. Robert Young, the guitarist, stepped back, so we began to stop writing songs based around guitar riffs, and started writing songs based around rhythm and atmosphere and texture.”
“Andrew Innes and I would go into the studio five days a week. On ‘Give Out But Don’t Give Up’ we reverted to a traditional band structure, but with The Bunker Trilogy that was cast to the wind.”
The highlights rank not only with the band’s best work, but challenge any other group working in that time period. Songs like ‘Star’ and ‘Kowalski’ took daring musicianship and production into the charts, built from the ground up in their tiny London studio. “I had things I wanted to express that I couldn’t express before because I was too inarticulate with language, and maybe too inarticulate with sound and song structure,” Bobby explains, “but the experience that we gathered, meant that we were in a position where we could actually finally make a statement that we’d always wanted to make.”
“We were able to realise something we’d always dreamed of doing by that point because we had the know-how, the expertise, the knowledge, the confidence, and the attitude.”
It helps that the guest cast contains some of British music’s most potent names. my bloody valentine maestro Kevin Shields joins for ‘XTRMNTR’, while the collapse of Manchester icons The Stone Roses saw bass player Mani join the group for a decade-long stint.
“Mani was a great bassist, a great musician,” the frontman notes. “But he was also this life-affirming, fun-love character. And he was very, very smart. He was a Grammar School boy – he went to the same Grammar School as Anthony Burgess, the guy that wrote A Clockwork Orange.” “Underneath that cheeky chappie Manc persona, Mani was a very smart guy. And we had so much fun, so many laughs… and he never played a bad gig.”
If the Bunker title is slightly tongue in cheek, it also reflects the band’s oppositional stance to British music at the time – the Britpop party was fading, stubbed out cigarettes were floating in glasses of flat champagne, and New Labour was firmly in power. “I think people like myself have been in opposition all our lives,” he says. “It was always this us and them attitude. That’s why we were punks when we were teenagers. We needed punk to articulate that, so we could realise we weren’t alone.”
“Britpop was very conservative music, so Primal Scream were definitely not part of that,” he says. “We just followed our hearts. We weren’t in competition with any other band.”
“We just had a different approach to every other band at the time,” he notes. “They were still writing and recording and producing records in the traditional manner that old rock groups did, but we deconstructed that and took a different approach.”
‘XTRMNTR’ lead single ‘Swastika Eyes’ wasn’t built for Radio 1 plays, as Bobby points out. “Radio stations weren’t going to play that song. We were being uncompromising, but that’s how we felt. It was what we wrote about, and if it’s unpalatable for daytime radio then so be it.”
“I kind of felt that at the end of the 90s you’d seen American bombers taking off from British airfields – because we’re kind of like an occupied country, aren’t we? We’re an aircraft carrier for the United States. The whole thing for me was, I think they’re gearing up for something bigger. This is just a dry run for something bigger.”
“And yes, that’s a dystopian view of the world, but I think it just came from the literature I was reading at the time, which was very paranoid. But I actually think I was on the money!”
That’s not to present this music as overly cerebral polemic – ‘Evil Heat’ in particular has moments of uplifting grace. Take Kate Moss’ angelic turn on a cover of ‘Some Velvet Morning’, for example. “We decided we were a track short,” he recalls, “so me and Andrew thought, let’s do a cover, and Kate can sing i.”
“Andrew wanted ‘Love Hurts’, the version by Gram Parsons and Emmylou Harris. I went for ‘Some Velvet Morning’. It was dissolute supermodel meets dissolute rock singer… but with electronics.”
There’s even a cameo from Led Zeppelin icon Robert Plant , who plays harmonica. “We met him in a pub after finishing the session with Kate Moss,” Bobby recalls. “Me being me, I just went up to him! I just said look, we’ve got this song which is a mixture between Throbbing Gristle and Howlin’ Wolf, do you want to play on it? And he did!”
Looking back doesn’t come easily to Bobby Gillespie. For one, some of the people mentioned aren’t with us any more – Mani passed away last year, for example. “I don’t sit about listening to old Primal Scream songs,” he points out during our chat. “I’m trying to write the newest Primal Scream song.”
“This re-issue gives me the chance to listen back to the albums, the B-sides… and I’ve got to say, I’m very proud of what we did. I think we wrote, produced, and released records with honour.”
“We did what a band is supposed to do: challenge themselves and challenge their audience.”
‘The Bunker trilogy’ is out now. Catch Primal Scream on the road this year.
Words: Robin Murray Photo Credit: Martina Hoogland Ivanow
items.title_zh: 逃离禁锢：Bobby Gillespie谈Primal Scream的无妥协时代
items.summary_zh: 本文讨论了Bobby Gillespie对Primal Scream乐队的看法，认为该乐队的音乐是对当时英国音乐的反叛。他强调，乐队成员始终追随内心的声音，而非与其他乐队竞争。Bobby Gillespie提到，在创作过程中，Primal Scream不受传统束缚，追求独特的音乐表达，力求创作出最新的Primal Scream歌曲。这种态度体现了他们对音乐的真诚和对艺术的坚持。
items.l1_lead: Primal Scream乐队通过追随内心声音和无拘无束的创作态度，展现了对音乐的真诚和对艺术的坚持，成为当时英国音乐的反叛象征。
items.l2_summary:
本文探讨了Bobby Gillespie对Primal Scream乐队的看法，强调该乐队的音乐是一种对当时英国音乐的反叛。Gillespie指出，Primal Scream的成员始终忠于内心的声音，而不是与其他乐队进行竞争。这种独特的创作理念使得他们在音乐创作过程中不受传统束缚，追求独特的音乐表达，力求创作出最新的Primal Scream歌曲。

Gillespie的观点反映了乐队对音乐的真诚态度和对艺术的坚持。他们的音乐不仅仅是为了迎合市场或流行趋势，而是源于对自我表达的渴望和对音乐本质的探索。这种无妥协的态度使得Primal Scream在音乐界中独树一帜，成为一种文化现象。

通过对Primal Scream的分析，Gillespie强调了艺术创作中的自由与个性的重要性，认为只有在摆脱外界压力和传统束缚的情况下，艺术家才能真正实现自我。这种理念不仅适用于音乐领域，也对其他艺术形式有着深远的影响，鼓励艺术家们勇于追求自己的创作道路，展现真实的自我。总之，Primal Scream的音乐不仅是对当时音乐环境的反叛，更是对艺术创作自由的坚定捍卫。

items.title_zh: 大脑如何预测现实
items.summary_zh: 本文探讨了科学家Karl Friston关于大脑如何通过最小化预测误差来理解现实的观点。Friston指出，有两种主要方式可以减少预测误差：一是通过改变思维，使得生成的预测更接近实际感知；二是通过行动来调整与环境的互动。这表明，思维和行动的变化都是有效的策略，可以帮助我们更准确地理解和适应周围的世界。通过这些方式，大脑能够更好地处理信息，从而提高对现实的预测能力。
items.l1_lead: 大脑通过调整思维和行动来最小化预测误差，从而更准确地理解和适应现实。
items.l2_summary:
本文探讨了科学家Karl Friston关于大脑如何通过最小化预测误差（prediction error）来理解现实的观点。研究指出，大脑在处理信息时，主要依赖于两种策略来减少预测误差。第一种策略是通过改变思维，使得大脑生成的预测更接近实际感知。这意味着，当我们的感知与预期不符时，大脑会调整其内部模型，以便更好地反映外部世界的真实状态。第二种策略则是通过行动来调整与环境的互动。通过主动参与和探索，个体能够获得更多的信息，从而修正其对现实的理解。

这一理论强调了思维和行动的变化都是有效的策略，能够帮助我们更准确地理解和适应周围的世界。通过不断地调整预测和实际感知之间的差距，大脑能够提高对现实的预测能力。这种机制不仅有助于我们在日常生活中做出更好的决策，也为理解人类行为和认知提供了重要的科学依据。

总的来说，Karl Friston的研究揭示了大脑在理解现实过程中的复杂性，强调了预测误差的最小化在认知和行为中的重要作用。这一发现为我们提供了新的视角，帮助我们理解大脑如何通过思维和行动的调整来适应不断变化的环境。

论据：这表明大脑通过生成假设来解释感官信息，从而最小化惊讶或预测误差。

items.l2_summary:
本文探讨了大脑作为构造性器官的观点，强调其在处理感官输入时的主动性，类似于一个统计引擎。核心论点是，大脑通过生成假设来解释感官信息，从而最小化惊讶（surprise）或预测误差（prediction error）。这一过程表明，大脑并不是被动地接收信息，而是积极地构建对现实的理解。研究表明，大脑在感知和认知过程中发挥着重要作用，尤其是在解释外部世界时展现出强大的预测能力。

通过这一机制，大脑能够有效地整合来自不同感官的信息，形成对环境的全面理解。具体而言，当大脑接收到感官输入时，它会根据以往的经验和知识生成多个假设，并通过比较这些假设与实际感官输入之间的差异来调整自身的理解。这种调整过程不仅提高了对现实的适应能力，还使得个体能够在复杂和动态的环境中做出快速反应。

此外，研究还指出，大脑的这种构造性机制在学习和记忆中起着关键作用。通过不断地更新和优化假设，大脑能够在面对新信息时迅速调整已有的认知框架，从而提高对新情况的适应能力。这一过程不仅涉及到感官信息的处理，还包括情感和社会认知等多方面的因素，进一步强调了大脑在复杂认知任务中的多功能性。

总之，本文揭示了大脑在感知和认知中的构造性机制，强调其在解释外部世界时的预测能力。这一观点不仅丰富了我们对大脑功能的理解，也为未来的研究提供了新的视角，可能会对认知科学、心理学以及人工智能等领域产生深远的影响。

items.summary_zh: 本文讨论了马克·索尔姆斯和卡尔·弗里斯顿对弗洛伊德观点的现代解读。核心论点是药物治疗本身无法改变思维，关键在于药物如何促进更有针对性的干预。作者指出，没有任何药物，包括迷幻药，能够单独改变一个人的思维。这一观点强调了药物在心理治疗中的辅助作用，而非主导作用，呼吁对药物治疗的理解应更加深入和全面。

items.l2_summary:
本文探讨了马克·索尔姆斯（Mark Solms）与卡尔·弗里斯顿（Karl Friston）对弗洛伊德（Sigmund Freud）观点的现代解读，提出了药物治疗在心理治疗中的辅助作用，而非主导作用的核心论点。作者强调，药物本身并不能改变思维，关键在于药物如何促进更有针对性的干预。具体而言，任何药物，包括迷幻药（psychedelics），都无法单独实现思维的转变，这一观点挑战了传统对药物治疗的理解。

在现代脑科学的背景下，索尔姆斯与弗里斯顿的研究为弗洛伊德的理论提供了新的视角，揭示了心理治疗中药物的作用机制。药物的使用应被视为一种工具，能够在特定的心理治疗框架内，帮助患者更有效地进行自我探索和情感处理。这种理解促使我们重新审视药物治疗的价值，强调了心理治疗师在干预过程中的重要性。

此外，文章还指出，药物治疗的效果往往依赖于患者的心理状态和治疗环境，而不仅仅是药物本身的化学成分。这一发现为心理治疗的实践提供了重要的指导，提示我们在进行药物治疗时，必须考虑到患者的个体差异和治疗的整体策略。

总之，索尔姆斯与弗里斯顿的研究不仅为弗洛伊德的理论提供了现代科学的支持，也促使我们对药物治疗的理解更加深入和全面，强调了心理治疗中人际关系和治疗环境的重要性。这一观点的提出，呼吁我们在未来的心理治疗实践中，注重药物与心理干预的结合，以实现更好的治疗效果。

items.title: Digital episodic memory tools for the identification of amnestic mild cognitive impairment: A systematic review and an exploratory meta-analysis.
items.body: Within our ageing population, the prevalence of Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment (aMCI) is rising, underscoring a need for early detection strategies to mitigate potential progression to dementia. Traditional pen-and-paper cognitive tests remain standard but often fail to capture subtle early impairments. Digital episodic memory tasks have emerged as a promising alternative, offering automated scoring, increased accessibility, and potentially better sensitivity to cognitive decline. We systematically evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of digital episodic memory assessments for aMCI. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria, with six (n = 510 participants) providing sufficient data for meta-analysis. Pooled estimates showed sensitivity of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.65-0.87), specificity of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.66-0.89), and AUC of 0.86, with low to moderate heterogeneity (I² = 36.1%), largely reflecting differences in task design and administration. Both quantitative and qualitative findings suggest digital episodic memory tasks can provide accessible, scalable, and effective tools for early aMCI detection. However, design variability and construct differences highlight the need for further validation across diverse populations and improved methodological standardisation before clinical implementation.
items.authors: Moura AR, Magalhães D, Dos Santos C, Marinho F, Henriques R, Wimmer GE, Dolan RJ, Fragata I.
items.title_zh: 数字化情节记忆工具在识别健忘型轻度认知障碍中的应用
items.summary_zh: 随着老龄化人口的增加，健忘型轻度认知障碍（aMCI）的发病率上升，迫切需要早期检测策略以减缓向痴呆的潜在进展。传统的纸笔认知测试虽然仍是标准，但常常无法捕捉到早期的微妙损害。数字化情节记忆任务作为一种有前景的替代方案，提供了自动评分、提高可及性以及对认知衰退的更好敏感性。我们系统评估了数字化情节记忆评估在aMCI诊断中的准确性。共有13项研究符合纳入标准，其中6项（n = 510参与者）提供了足够的数据进行荟萃分析。汇总结果显示敏感性为0.78（95% CI: 0.65-0.87），特异性为0.79（95% CI: 0.66-0.89），曲线下面积（AUC）为0.86，异质性低至中等（I² = 36.1%），主要反映任务设计和实施的差异。定量和定性结果均表明，数字化情节记忆任务可以为早期aMCI检测提供可及、可扩展和有效的工具。然而，设计的变异性和构念差异强调了在临床实施前，需要在不同人群中进一步验证和改进方法标准化的必要性。
items.l1_lead: 数字化情节记忆工具在识别健忘型轻度认知障碍中表现出良好的敏感性和特异性，提供了一种可及且有效的早期检测方案，但需进一步验证和标准化。
items.l2_summary:
随着全球老龄化人口的不断增加，健忘型轻度认知障碍（aMCI）的发病率也在上升，这使得早期检测策略的需求愈发迫切，以期减缓其向痴呆的潜在进展。传统的纸笔认知测试虽然仍然是标准方法，但往往无法有效捕捉到早期的微妙损害。因此，数字化情节记忆任务作为一种新兴的替代方案，展现出了良好的前景。该方法不仅提供了自动评分的便利性，还提高了测试的可及性，并对认知衰退表现出更高的敏感性。

在对数字化情节记忆评估在aMCI诊断中的准确性进行系统评估时，共有13项研究符合纳入标准，其中6项研究（共510名参与者）提供了足够的数据进行荟萃分析。汇总结果显示，该数字化评估工具的敏感性为0.78（95% CI: 0.65-0.87），特异性为0.79（95% CI: 0.66-0.89），曲线下面积（AUC）为0.86，且异质性低至中等（I² = 36.1%），这主要反映了任务设计和实施过程中的差异。

定量和定性结果均表明，数字化情节记忆任务能够为早期aMCI的检测提供一种可及、可扩展且有效的工具。然而，研究中任务设计的变异性和构念差异也强调了在临床实施前，必须在不同人群中进一步验证和改进方法的标准化。这一发现为未来的研究和临床应用提供了重要的参考，表明数字化工具在认知障碍早期检测中的潜力与挑战并存。

items.title: The prenatal sex steroid theory of autism after 25 years.
items.body: We first proposed the prenatal sex steroid theory of autism 25 years ago to account for a number of then-unexplained observations around autism, including (1) the more frequent diagnosis of autism in male than in female individuals and (2) apparent 'male-type' shifts in cognitive traits associated with autism, such as empathizing and systemizing. Here we review 25 years of research testing this theory. Early studies found that higher prenatal testosterone levels were associated with slower social, language and empathy development, greater attention to detail, stronger systemizing and more autistic traits. Subsequent studies suggested that both prenatal androgens and oestrogens are associated with autism. New methods in genetics and using stem-cell-derived neural organoids have further indicated the importance of sex steroid hormones for neurodevelopment, as well as atypical patterns in autism. These new findings support and open new lines of research into the prenatal sex steroid theory of autism.

items.title_zh: 产前性激素理论与自闭症研究25年回顾
items.summary_zh: 本文回顾了产前性激素理论在自闭症研究中的发展历程，提出该理论以解释自闭症相关的观察现象，包括男性自闭症患者的比例高于女性，以及与自闭症相关的认知特征（如共情和系统化）的“男性化”倾向。早期研究发现，较高的产前睾酮水平与社交、语言和共情发展缓慢、对细节的关注度提高、系统化能力增强及更多自闭症特征相关。后续研究表明，产前雄激素（androgens）和雌激素（oestrogens）均与自闭症相关。最新的遗传学方法和干细胞衍生的神经类器官研究进一步强调了性激素在神经发育中的重要性，以及自闭症中的非典型模式。这些新发现支持了产前性激素理论，并为未来的研究开辟了新方向。
items.l1_lead: 产前性激素理论在自闭症研究中逐渐得到支持，揭示了性激素在神经发育和自闭症特征形成中的重要作用。
items.l2_summary:
本文回顾了产前性激素理论在自闭症研究中的发展历程，探讨了该理论如何解释自闭症相关的观察现象，尤其是男性自闭症患者的比例显著高于女性，以及与自闭症相关的认知特征（如共情和系统化）的“男性化”倾向。早期研究发现，较高的产前睾酮（testosterone）水平与社交、语言和共情发展缓慢、对细节的关注度提高、系统化能力增强及更多自闭症特征相关。这些发现为理解自闭症的性别差异提供了生物学基础。

后续研究进一步表明，产前雄激素（androgens）和雌激素（oestrogens）均与自闭症的发生相关，提示性激素在自闭症的发病机制中扮演着重要角色。最新的遗传学方法和干细胞衍生的神经类器官研究，强调了性激素在神经发育过程中的关键作用，揭示了自闭症中的非典型神经发育模式。这些新发现不仅支持了产前性激素理论，还为未来的研究开辟了新的方向，提示研究者在探索自闭症的生物学基础时，需考虑性激素的影响。

综上所述，产前性激素理论为理解自闭症提供了重要的生物学视角，尤其是在解释性别差异和认知特征方面。随着研究的深入，未来可能会有更多关于性激素与自闭症关系的发现，为自闭症的早期识别和干预提供新的思路。

Arday, who resigned after a plagiarism row, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to his home in Battersea, London, just after 3pm on Friday to reports that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.
The Metropolitan Police said his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.
University of Cambridge professor and director of the Autism Research Centre Simon Baron-Cohen told the BBC he spoke to Arday on Friday morning.
Baron-Cohen told Radio 4’s Today programme: “He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.”
“He used those words in voice notes,” he added.
Baron-Cohen said: “At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.
“He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager, and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way.”
Baron-Cohen said Arday was a “kind and gentle” man who had been “bombarded by every media outlet” and used as a “lightning rod” to examine diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.
Arday, a professor of sociology of education who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, quit following a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.
Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million (€6.44 million) for charity.
An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Arday of wrongdoing.
Baron-Cohen told the BBC that plagiarism allegations made by another academic, Nathan Cofnas – who has reportedly defined himself as a “race realist” – opened up a “media frenzy”.
He said: “Jason was being used as almost like a lightning rod to examine this policy of DEI, and Jason was bombarded by every media outlet to paint him as a fraud.”
The cognitive neuroscientist said he had grown concerned about the mental health of Arday, a “vulnerable autistic man” that he could see was struggling.
Baron-Cohen said: “In the last 10 days, I’ve witnessed his mental health getting worse and worse, as the media didn’t stop ridiculing him, humiliating him, discrediting him.
“As I said, yesterday morning, his last voice note was that he just couldn’t go on.
“We need to let the investigations proceed, we need to understand how this tragedy has happened, but there has to be accountability at lots of levels.”
In a statement on Saturday, National Education Union (NEU) general secretary Daniel Kebede said Arday had been subjected to “a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism”.
He added: “I don’t believe this was ever simply about ‘professional conduct’ or ‘plagiarism’.
“There is a profound difference between scrutiny and a sustained public campaign that turns an individual into a symbol of everything the right believes is wrong with DEI.
“The effect has been chilling. It tells black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target.
“A target not only for criticism of your work, but for a much broader political and cultural backlash.”
Speaking to reporters while on a visit to southwest England, UK prime minister Andy Burnham said it was “not a moment for any rushing to judgement”.
“It’s a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends — we think of them today,” the British leader said.
“It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how how things came to this,” he added.
Over the weekend, Arday cancelled events promoting his forthcoming memoir.
Publisher Simon & Schuster previously said that the book, Great And Unfortunate Things, would be published in the UK on 27 August.
In a statement on Saturday, the publisher said: “Simon & Schuster is deeply saddened by the news of Jason Arday’s tragic death, and we send our condolences to his family during this devastating time.”

items.title_zh: 剑桥前教授Jason Arday临终前感到无法继续生活
items.summary_zh: Jason Arday，前剑桥大学教授，因媒体的持续攻击而心理健康恶化。在他去世前的几个小时，他向朋友表示自己“无法继续下去”。Arday在童年时被诊断出患有自闭症、语言延迟和学习差异等障碍。在过去的十天里，媒体不断对他进行嘲笑、羞辱和抹黑，导致他的心理状态急剧恶化。最终，这些压力使他感到无法承受，选择结束自己的生命。
items.l1_lead: 媒体的持续攻击严重影响了前剑桥教授Jason Arday的心理健康，最终导致他选择结束自己的生命。
items.l2_summary:
前剑桥大学教授Jason Arday在临终前感到无法继续生活，原因在于他遭受了媒体的持续攻击，导致心理健康状况急剧恶化。Arday在童年时期被诊断出患有自闭症（autism）、语言延迟（language delay）和学习差异（learning differences）等障碍，这些问题使他的生活和学术生涯面临诸多挑战。在他去世前的几个小时，他向朋友表达了自己的绝望，表示“无法继续下去”。在过去的十天里，媒体对他的嘲笑、羞辱和抹黑不断升级，这种持续的心理压力最终使他感到无法承受，选择结束自己的生命。

这一悲剧突显了媒体对个体心理健康的影响，尤其是对于那些本就面临挑战的人群。Arday的经历提醒我们，社会对心理健康问题的关注和理解仍然不足，尤其是在面对自闭症和其他学习障碍时。媒体的负面报道不仅对个人造成伤害，也反映了社会对这些问题的偏见和误解。Arday的故事是一个警示，呼吁我们在讨论和报道心理健康问题时，需更加谨慎和同情，以免加重当事人的痛苦。

items.article_body:
Coffee House Melanie McDonagh The tragedy of Jason Arday Saturday, August 15, 2026, 10:30 AM Jason Arday (Credit: BBC) Text settings Text size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious Comments Share Share Melanie McDonagh
Copied Linkedin Messenger Email Simon Baron-Cohen, the distinguished Cambridge autism specialist, has been speaking movingly about his friend, Jason Arday, in a BBC radio interview. Baron-Cohen said the last contact he had with Arday was hours before he was found dead at an address in south London yesterday afternoon: “He really wasn’t coping. He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny… ridicule, discrediting every detail of his life… He wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation. He felt he couldn’t go on.”
Jason Arday was a victim, but not in the way that his political champions suggest
Baron-Cohen went on to talk about him as “an incredibly kind and gentle and caring and generous man”. From his own perspective, he observed, “at the heart of all this was a man who was diagnosed with autism and language differences…he needed support every step of the way… after the allegations of plagiarism, [the] media didn’t leave him alone.”
It is good to be reminded of Jason Arday as a friend, by a friend. For in death we all should be remembered in our humanity, even in our flawed humanity. And Jason Arday was very human; he bled. He was not just a totem of DEI (Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion), but as the Prof said, a vulnerable man. It’s sometimes hard for pundits, self included, to remember how terrifying it is to be at the heart of a media firestorm. Jason Arday isn’t the first to feel the pressure to be unbearable. We may not feel exactly guilt at participating in the row, but it would be strange if we didn’t feel sober, chastened, by his tragic end.
De mortuis nil nisi bonum is a good motto, but in Arday’s case, the difficulty about speaking no evil of the dead is in disentangling the man, the human being, from the issue. And the issue was quite legitimate: the apparent dearth of scrutiny of his successive appointments, the uncritical and unquestioned acceptance of his work and his claims as, for instance, a fundraiser. His family, in their pain, has talked about him as the victim of misinformation. This isn’t, I would say, the whole case, though this isn’t the time to rehearse the details.
Before his death becomes weaponized – as it already risks being – in the culture wars, we should make one thing clear, as I, in fact, did before he died. It is that the problem was not Jason Arday; it was with the individuals who lionized him, who promoted him beyond his capacities, who raised him up prematurely to stellar heights at an age which would have been remarkable for anyone, regardless of ethnicity. It is the individuals behind the system which created Jason Arday, the poster image of DEI, who should be asking themselves some questions.
Arday can hardly be blamed for not resisting this inexorable trajectory. And, I would say, the fault is with Cambridge for making a dud subject like Education a faculty on the same level as history or natural sciences or classics. Jason Arday was a victim, but not quite in the way that his political champions suggest.
He was also a man, a father, a son, a brother and an uncle, as his family have said, and it is as such he is being mourned. Requiescat in pace.
Melanie McDonagh is an Irish journalist working in London.

items.title_zh: 杰森·阿尔代的悲剧
items.summary_zh: 本文讨论了杰森·阿尔代在面对媒体持续压力和职业生涯丧失时的困境。阿尔代被诊断为自闭症（autism）和语言障碍（language differences），在经历抄袭指控后，他感到无法承受来自媒体的无情审视和嘲笑，缺乏必要的支持。他失去了职业和声誉，内心深处感到绝望，认为自己无法继续前行。文章强调了在这种情况下，社会对有特殊需求人士的支持和理解的重要性。
items.l1_lead: 杰森·阿尔代因媒体压力和职业危机感到绝望，突显了社会对特殊需求人士支持与理解的重要性。
items.l2_summary:
杰森·阿尔代的悲剧揭示了在媒体压力和职业生涯丧失的双重打击下，特殊需求人士所面临的困境。阿尔代被诊断为自闭症（autism）和语言障碍（language differences），这使他在面对外界的审视时显得更加脆弱。在经历了抄袭指控后，媒体的持续关注和无情的嘲笑让他感到无所适从，缺乏必要的支持与理解。他的职业生涯因此受到重创，声誉也随之崩塌，内心深处的绝望感愈发加重，令他认为自己无法继续前行。

文章强调了社会对有特殊需求人士的支持和理解的重要性，指出在面对困境时，缺乏适当的帮助和关怀可能会导致更严重的心理和情感问题。阿尔代的经历不仅是个人的悲剧，更是对社会如何对待特殊需求人士的深刻反思。通过他的故事，读者能够感受到在职业生涯和个人生活中，理解与支持的重要性，以及在面对困难时，社会应当提供怎样的帮助。杰森·阿尔代的遭遇提醒我们，只有通过建立一个更具包容性和理解的环境，才能真正帮助那些在逆境中挣扎的人们。

items.article_body:
Jason Arday was found dead at his home in south London on Friday. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Jason Arday was found dead at his home in south London on Friday. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian Jason Arday This article is more than 1 month old Tributes paid to Jason Arday after former Cambridge professor’s death This article is more than 1 month old Andy Burnham calls for reflection after ‘tragedy on so many levels’ in comments echoed by London mayor Sadiq Khan
Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has called the death of Jason Arday , whose body was found at his home in south London on Friday, a “tragedy on so many levels”.
Arday resigned as a professor at the University of Cambridge last week after allegations of plagiarism, which he denied. He was pronounced dead just after 3pm on Friday .
In a statement issued via his publisher, Simon & Schuster UK, the former academic’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.
Speaking to broadcasters during a visit to Cornwall on Saturday, the prime minister said: “It’s a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends. We think of them today.
“It’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this. A really sad, sad and sorry state of affairs and I think we all today think of Jason, his contribution and his family and friends.”
More than £20,000 has been raised for the family of Arday after the Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon launched a fundraising drive via GoFundMe in his memory.
Other leading figures to pay tribute included the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, and the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy.
Khan said: “I’m devastated for the family and friends of Jason Arday. He faced an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse. I know many Londoners will be angry and upset this evening.
“Jason Arday was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake-up call for all of us.”
Speaking on Newsnight, Ribeiro-Addy read out a list of names including William O’Reilly, Ros Holmes, David Latchman, and Nicola Morrison. “These are all people that have actually proven to have been plagiarists, or people that have manipulated their data, and people that have been proven to have lifted whole pages from students’ papers or published work that they had to withdraw,” she said.
Ribeiro-Addy said there had been a media witch-hunt which was cruel because “it didn’t aim to just target him”.
“It aimed to target anybody that supported him, trying to isolate him as much as possible, going after people who had signed up to statements,” she said. “The difference between them and him was they were white, and he was not.”
The Conservative MP James Cleverly expressed his anger over Arday’s death. In a statement on X, he wrote that a number of people at academic institutions “have serious questions to answer”.
“They put him into positions he was clearly not qualified for so they could have a black wunderkind to show off, they pushed him into the spotlight for their own benefit,” they said. “His exposure was inevitable, a case of when, not if. His whole world fell apart.”
Simon Baron-Cohen, a clinical psychologist and the director of the Autism Research Centre, who was a friend of Arday’s, told Radio 4’s Today programme that he contacted him Friday morning and said that he felt he was unable to go on.
“He used those words in voice notes,” Baron-Cohen said. “At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.
“He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way.”

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters
Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another person’s work in his PhD thesis, but denied all allegations. A review conducted by Liverpool John Moores University, where he completed his doctorate, upheld its decision to award him a PhD earlier this year.
In recent weeks, other elements of his life story were increasingly questioned , including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running. He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal as a child.
The National Education Union general secretary, Daniel Kebede, said Arday had been subjected to “a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism”.
“I don’t believe this was ever simply about ‘professional conduct’ or ‘plagiarism’,” he said.
“There is a profound difference between scrutiny and a sustained public campaign that turns an individual into a symbol of everything the right believes is wrong with DEI.
“The effect has been chilling. It tells Black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target.
“A target not only for criticism of your work, but for a much broader political and cultural backlash.”
The Metropolitan police said his death was being treated as unexpected, but not believed to be suspicious.

items.title_zh: 阿尔代：脆弱个体的保护与支持
items.summary_zh: 文章讨论了已故剑桥大学教授阿尔代的成长经历，强调他在童年时期被诊断出自闭症、语言延迟和学习差异等障碍。作者指出，阿尔代作为一个脆弱的孩子、青少年和成年人，始终需要并应当得到保护、支持和合理的调整。文章的核心论点是，社会应为像阿尔代这样的脆弱个体提供必要的保障，以确保他们在成长过程中能够获得平等的机会和支持。
items.l1_lead: 社会应为脆弱个体提供必要的保护与支持，以确保他们在成长过程中获得平等的机会和合理的调整。
items.l2_summary:
阿尔代（Alday）是已故剑桥大学教授，他的成长经历为我们提供了对脆弱个体保护与支持的重要思考。文章指出，阿尔代在童年时期被诊断出自闭症（Autism）、语言延迟（Language Delay）和学习差异（Learning Differences），这些障碍使他在生活的各个阶段都面临着挑战。作为一个脆弱的孩子、青少年和成年人，阿尔代始终需要保护和支持，这不仅是他个人的需求，也是社会应承担的责任。

文章的核心论点强调，社会应为像阿尔代这样的脆弱个体提供必要的保障，以确保他们在成长过程中能够获得平等的机会和支持。阿尔代的经历表明，缺乏适当的支持和合理的调整，脆弱个体可能会面临更大的困难和孤立。因此，社会各界应当关注这些个体的需求，提供必要的资源和环境，以帮助他们克服障碍，实现自我价值。

通过对阿尔代的成长故事的分析，作者呼吁社会重视脆弱个体的权益，倡导建立一个包容的环境，使每一个人都能在平等的基础上获得发展机会。这样的支持不仅有助于脆弱个体的成长，也将促进整个社会的和谐与进步。总之，阿尔代的经历提醒我们，保护和支持脆弱个体是社会的共同责任，只有通过集体的努力，才能为他们创造一个更加友好的生活和学习环境。

items.article_body:
David Hughes | Izzie Addison | Michael Howie , Senior News Editor 15 August 2026 News Briefings

Andy Burnham has called the death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday a “tragedy” that should be a “moment for reflection”.
Prof Arday, who resigned after a plagiarism row, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday to reports that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.
He told a friend he “couldn’t go on” hours before he died after being subjected to intense scrutiny over his academic career.
The Prime Minister told reporters during a visit to Cornwall: “It’s a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends. We think of think of them today.
“It’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how how things came to this.
“A really sad, sad and sorry state of affairs and I think we all today think of Jason, his contribution, and his family and friends.”
Jason Arday was found dead on Friday ES Prof Arday said he felt he “couldn’t go on” hours before he died, a friend revealed earlier on Saturday.
Prof Arday was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to Daley Thompson Way, in Battersea , just after 3pm on Friday to reports that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.
The Metropolitan Police said his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.
Prof Arday last week resigned as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge .
A series of media reports alleged he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.
Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million for charity.

An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Prof Arday of wrongdoing.
University of Cambridge professor, and director of the Autism Research Centre, Sir Simon Baron-Cohen told the BBC he spoke to Prof Arday on Friday morning.
Jason Arday was a professor of sociology of education at Cambridge University AFP/Getty Sir Simon told Radio 4’s Today programme: “He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.”
“He used those words in voice notes,” he added.
Sir Simon said: “At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.
“He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager, and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way.”
Sir Simon said Prof Arday was a “kind and gentle” man who had been “bombarded by every media outlet” and used as a “lightning rod” to examine diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.
Sir Simon told the BBC that plagiarism allegations made by another academic, Nathan Cofnas – who has reportedly defined himself as a “race realist” – opened up a “media frenzy”.
He said: “Jason was being used as almost like a lightning rod to examine this policy of DEI, and Jason was bombarded by every media outlet to paint him as a fraud.”
The cognitive neuroscientist said he had grown concerned about the mental health of Prof Arday, a “vulnerable autistic man” that he could see was struggling.
Andy Burnham spoke about Jason Arday’s tragic death on a visit to Cornwall on Saturday PA Sir Simon said: “In the last 10 days, I’ve witnessed his mental health getting worse and worse, as the media didn’t stop ridiculing him, humiliating him, discrediting him.
“As I said, yesterday morning, his last voice note was that he just couldn’t go on.
“We need to let the investigations proceed, we need to understand how this tragedy has happened, but there has to be accountability at lots of levels.”
In a statement on Saturday, National Education Union (NEU) general secretary Daniel Kebede said Prof Arday had been subjected to “a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism”.
He added: “I don’t believe this was ever simply about ‘professional conduct’ or ‘plagiarism’.
“There is a profound difference between scrutiny and a sustained public campaign that turns an individual into a symbol of everything the right believes is wrong with DEI.
“The effect has been chilling. It tells black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target.
“A target not only for criticism of your work, but for a much broader political and cultural backlash.”

items.title_zh: 前剑桥教授杰森·阿尔代去世引发的多重悲剧
items.summary_zh: 杰森·阿尔代（Jason Arday）因职业和声誉的丧失而感到无法继续生活。他在生前遭受了无情的审视，包括嘲笑和对他生活每个细节的抹黑，导致他无法应对失去事业和声誉的痛苦。正如一位评论者所言，他感到无法继续前行，这反映了学术界对个人生活的影响及其潜在的悲剧性后果。阿尔代的去世不仅是个人的悲剧，也引发了对学术环境中压力和心理健康问题的深刻反思。
items.l1_lead: 杰森·阿尔代的去世揭示了学术界对个人生活的影响及其导致的心理健康危机，反映出职业压力可能引发的悲剧性后果。
items.l2_summary: 杰森·阿尔代（Jason Alday）的去世引发了对学术界压力和心理健康问题的深刻反思。他在生前因职业和声誉的丧失而感到绝望，无法继续生活。阿尔代遭受了无情的审视，包括嘲笑和对他生活每个细节的抹黑，这些都加剧了他对失去事业和声誉的痛苦。正如一位评论者所指出的，他感到无法继续前行，这一现象反映了学术界对个人生活的影响及其潜在的悲剧性后果。阿尔代的去世不仅是他个人的悲剧，也揭示了学术环境中普遍存在的压力和心理健康问题，促使人们重新审视这一领域对学者的影响。学术界的竞争和对个人生活的过度关注，可能导致严重的心理健康问题，甚至悲剧的发生。阿尔代的经历提醒我们，学术界需要更加关注研究人员的心理健康，创造一个更为支持和理解的环境，以防止类似悲剧的重演。

items.title: UK's leader calls for reflection after the death of former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism - Yahoo News Canada
items.body:
原话：“He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn't coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation.”
论点：他认为学术界对个体的审查和批评可能导致严重的心理影响。
items.attribution_basis: Google News 全名命中 + LLM 同一人核验（Yahoo News Canada） + 论点方向独立复核
quotes: He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn't coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation.
items.claim_zh: 他认为学术界对个体的审查和批评可能导致严重的心理影响。
items.article_body:
LONDON (AP) — Britain's prime minister called for reflection on Saturday after a Black professor who faced a storm of plagiarism accusations died suddenly, days after resigning from a prestigious role at the University of Cambridge.
Jason Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest Black professor in 2023, was found dead inside an address in south London on Friday. He resigned last week as professor of sociology of education after coming under intense media scrutiny , with weeks of news headlines alleging plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.
His death has prompted outcries that the allegations against Arday, 41, were magnified into a cruel public takedown motivated by racism and longstanding hostility to diversity, equity and inclusion, or DEI, policies at universities and other institutions.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Arday's death was "a tragedy on so many levels."
"It's not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It's a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this," Burnham told reporters.
Arday's family says he suffered years of abuse and harassment
Police said the death was being treated as "unexpected" but not suspicious. They said officers were called to an address in south London on Friday afternoon and a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. They did not name Arday, in accordance with police policy.
A friend said Arday had told him that he "felt he couldn't go on" in a voice note earlier Friday.
"He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn't coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation," Cambridge professor and director of the Autism Research Centre, Simon Baron-Cohen, told the BBC.
Arday's family said in a statement that he had been subjected to a "campaign of harassment" and "sustained abuse" ever since he took up his post as professor at Cambridge.
"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason," the family said in a statement issued through his publisher Simon & Schuster U.K. "We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."
Cambridge vice chancellor Deborah Prentice, who earlier announced that the university will investigate the circumstances around Arday's employment, said she was "desperately saddened" by the news.
Cambridge had opened investigations into plagiarism
Questions about Arday's qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a one-time Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his critique of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests. Cofnas previously argued that in a meritocracy, Black people "would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment."
Newspapers soon published stories alleging that more than 100 passages from Arday's 2015 Ph.D. thesis were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.
British media then raised wider questions about many of Arday's claims about his life, including statements he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($7.4 million) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days. Arday later revised those claims.
Some also questioned his claim that he had overcome developmental delays that left him non-verbal until the age of 11. Arday said he was diagnosed with autism at a young age and didn't read or write at 18 years old.
Arday resigned from Cambridge on Aug. 5. He denied plagiarism, but admitted to some mistakes when working on his doctorate.
Dozens of Cambridge academics signed a letter calling for an independent inquiry into how Arday was appointed. Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.
The university then changed its stance and said it had opened an investigation "following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."
Prentice, the university's vice chancellor, said this week she shared concerns regarding his appointment and that Cambridge will run a review of how it hires senior staff.
Criticism of Arday became part of broader culture wars
While some believe Arday was a victim of media "hounding" and racism, others say there are more complex issues at play — including whether Cambridge made the right call when it appointed Arday to such a high-profile position.
Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the National Education Union, said questions about Arday's credibility "unleashed a tirade of racism."
"There is a profound difference between scrutiny and a sustained public campaign that turns an individual into a symbol of everything the right believes is wrong with DEI," he said. "The effect has been chilling. It tells Black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target."
London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced."
Former Conservative home secretary James Cleverly, who is Black, wrote on X that academic institutions "have serious questions to answer."
"They put him into positions he was clearly not qualified for so they could have a Black wunderkind to show off; they pushed him into the spotlight for their own benefit," he said.

items.article_body:
We use cookies where necessary to allow us to understand how people interact with our website and content, so that we can continue to improve our service.
There cannot be any doubt that Dr Arday’s tragic death was the direct, foreseeable and foreseen result of press harassment. A significant element in that harassment was the colour of his skin. Self-regulation of the press has comprehensively failed.
Several weeks ago, Simon Baron-Cohen, director of Cambridge University’s Autism Research centre, warned publicly that “1 in 4 autistic people have planned or attempted suicide” and talked of the “relentless bullying of a vulnerable autistic man” which “raises safe-guarding issues”. Many of the signatories to this letter warned multiple media outlets privately that their relentless pursuit of Dr Arday risked his suicide.
Two weeks of relentless harassment followed, continuing even after his resignation as a Professor when the reasonable public interest in the story had diminished or evaporated. On 14 August, Dr Arday died in the most tragic circumstances. His tragic death did not result from the allegations of plagiarism but from the press coverage.
There cannot be any doubt that racism lay at the heart of this story.
Dr Arday was a relatively obscure figure outside of academia. Far more consequential figures, in whom there was a profound public interest, like Rachel Reeves and Jonathan Reynolds faced plausible allegations of embellishing their CVs or plagiarism. But the stories garnered relatively little coverage. When the academic Professor George Holmes – not merely a Professor but a Vice Chancellor – was implicated in a fraud scandal the story was barely covered. So too when William O’Reilly, another Professor at the University of Cambridge, faced plausible allegations of plagiarising student essays, again, there was very little in the media. When the Prime Minister of Canada, Mark Carney, faced plagiarism allegations they, also, received a tiny fraction of the coverage given to Dr Arday.
What those stories had in common is that they were about white people.
The harassment of public figures because of the colour of their skin is not unique to Dr Arday. Misan Harriman, Diane Abbott, Eniola Aluko, Jameela Jamil, Halima Begum and others have experienced press harassment with racist overtones. To be Black and a public figure is now enough to make you a target.
Black people are fearful and on the evidence they are right to be.
The years since the Leveson inquiry have taught us that the press is not interested in self-regulation. IPSO has failed. Lessons that should have been learned from the tragic deaths of Lucy Meadows and then Caroline Flack were not learned. Instead of getting better, press conduct is getting worse. And the impact of that failure is deadly.
We respectfully ask you to commission an immediate public inquiry into how to ensure a responsible press given its contribution to Dr Arday’s tragic death.

items.title: Jason Arday death 'tragedy on so many levels' says PM - BBC
items.body:
原话：“He was an incredibly, kind and gentle and caring man.”
论点：Jason Arday是一个非常善良和温柔的人。
items.attribution_basis: Google News 全名命中 + LLM 同一人核验（BBC） + 论点方向独立复核
quotes: He was an incredibly, kind and gentle and caring man.
items.claim_zh: Jason Arday是一个非常善良和温柔的人。
items.article_body:
Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ruth Comerford Death of Jason Arday 'a tragedy on so many levels', says PM Andy Burnham has described the death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday as "a tragedy on so many levels", as he called for a "moment for reflection".
Arday was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.
"It's not a moment for any rushing to judgement. It's a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this," the prime minister told broadcasters during a visit to Cornwall.
In a statement issued by his publisher Simon & Schuster UK, Arday's family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".
They said a "campaign of misinformation" had been too much for him.
Arday, 41, resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.
A friend told the BBC Arday had described feeling "destroyed" and had told him his authorisation to travel to the US had been revoked.
Eamonn McCrystal, who became his friend at St Mary's University, Twickenham, tried to reassure him what he was going through would pass, but Arday replied "it does not feel like it will."
McCrystal told the BBC "He was the nicest person. So kind and such a gentle soul.
"We shared an office at university, when I set up the student radio station, and he used to speak on the station a lot."
The University of Cambridge vice-chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice led the tributes, saying the faculty was "desperately saddened" to learn of his death.
"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she added.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" and urged people to "remember there are real people with loved ones involved".
Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan said Arday was subjected to unrelenting media scrutiny.
He said he had faced "an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse" and was the victim of "a pernicious public shaming".
"His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us," he posted on X.
A donation page, set up by Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon, has raised more than £10,000 to help cover funeral costs for Arday's family.
"Today should be about compassion, dignity and solidarity with a grieving family," Vernon wrote.
"Jason's life was bigger than the controversy that surrounded his final weeks."
A vigil will be held on Monday evening on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, held by the organisation Stand Up To Racism.
The group's co-convenor, Weyman Bennett, said Arday's death "was the result of a racist witch hunt".
Jo Grady, general secretary of the University and College Union, said the "level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to has been sickening" and "must be investigated".
Lord Paul Boateng, who became the UK's first black cabinet minister in 2002, told BBC Newsnight he was "horrified, shocked and deeply saddened".
"Racism in academia is a fact of life and needs to be addressed," he added in a written statement.
In a statement on Saturday, National Education Union general secretary Daniel Kebede said Arday had been subjected to "a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism".
"The effect has been chilling. It tells black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target," he said.
Prof Simon Baron-Cohen, director of the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme Arday had been "bombarded by every media outlet to paint him as a fraud".
"He was an incredibly, kind and gentle and caring man," he said.
He spoke to Arday the morning of his death, and said the academic had felt unable to leave the house.
"He has experienced what he described as a campaign against him, for the last three years," he previously told BBC News.
"What he was saying to me was 'they've destroyed my life' - it's not clear who they were but I think he was referring to the media.
"The personal attacks on him have been so immense."
Former colleague of Arday says they spoke on morning of his death Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, described him as "very down" after resigning from Cambridge.
"He was very upset. He felt that there was no way out. He effectively wasn't leaving the house. He had lost a lot of weight," Andrews said.
"There should be a wakeup call to just how bad black academics actually have it in academia."
Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy also told the programme "the idea that an academic would be dragged through this amount of media scrutiny is unheard of".
On Saturday Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said that people who "made many hard comments must now consider the impact of their words", describing it as a "deeply concerning and very sad case".
Prior to his appointment at Cambridge, Arday had worked as a professor at the University of Glasgow.
Shadow communities secretary Sir James Cleverly said he was angered by the "tragic" death and said "a number of people at a number of academic institutions have serious questions to answer".
When asked by the BBC on Saturday if the University of Cambridge needed to answer questions over its duty of care, Cleverly said the university should "ask themselves how he got into this position, how he ended up being in the eye of the storm, what could and should have happened to prevent this long before it got to this tragic situation".
Arday had denied plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and said the recent controversy had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".
The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.
Arday said some errors in his early academic work arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.
Questions were also raised about parts of his life story, including that he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5m for charity.
He later said the run was actually completed over a 12-day period to allow for rest days - and that the huge sum was raised with the help of others.
Arday's appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time.
Announcing his resignation last week, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny of him had become "too great".
He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.
"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."
He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".
Earlier this week, Cambridge announced an independent investigation around the circumstances of Arday's appointment.
Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.
In a statement on Saturday, a spokesperson for the university said it was "saddened to hear of the tragic loss of Professor Jason Arday".

George Brown: the former Post Office boy who unlocked the mystery of depression
Derek Owusu: ‘I’ve never figured out how to live in the world’
Two weeks ago, following a conversation with Jason Arday, Professor Simon Baron-Cohen posted a message on X.
The psychologist said he was “very concerned” about the impact of media coverage on his friend, who had autism, and linked it to work his Autism Research Centre at Cambridge University had done showing that autistic people were at a greater risk of suicide.
“This is relentless bullying of a vulnerable autistic man and raises safe-guarding issues,” he wrote. “It’s time to stop.” The site’s owner, Elon Musk, responded to the post with one word: “Liar”.
Yesterday, Baron-Cohen said Arday had sent him a voice note via WhatsApp on the morning of his death. “He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with… he felt he couldn’t go on,” he told Radio 4’s Today programme.
In 2022, Baron-Cohen and psychologists from other UK universities found that autistic people had an elevated risk of suicide. They examined 372 coroners’ inquest reports over a three-year period to find out whether the person who died had been diagnosed with autism or had autistic traits. They found evidence of autism in more than 10% of those who died, compared with about 1.1% of the population overall.
Jill Aylott, founder of the National Autism and ADHD Assessment Centre, said: “accountability should never require us to abandon humanity.
“When somebody becomes the focus of sustained national criticism, particularly where that person is known to be neurodivergent, institutions should be asking: who is checking that this person is safe?”
Baron-Cohen said that for the last 10 days he had seen Arday’s mental health “getting worse and worse”.

Derek Owusu: ‘I’ve never figured out how to live in the world’
“We need to let the investigations proceed. We need to understand how this tragedy has happened, but there has to be accountability at lots of levels.”

items.topic_zh: 对大学调查的支持及对媒体责任的质疑
items.claim_zh: 他认为大学应继续调查，以了解更多信息，并质疑媒体对阿尔代的照顾责任。
items.article_body:
Jason Arday quit his role as professor of sociology of education this month. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Jason Arday quit his role as professor of sociology of education this month. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian Jason Arday This article is more than 1 month old Cambridge University defends its mental health support for Jason Arday This article is more than 1 month old University says it continued to provide support after resignation of academic, who was found dead on Friday
Prefer the Guardian on Google The University of Cambridge has defended its mental health support for the academic Jason Arday.
The university said it had continued to provide Arday with extensive mental health support and security measures, including installing panic alarms and screening racist emails and post, after he resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education this month.
He quit after widespread press coverage of accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements .
A University of Cambridge spokesperson said: “Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason’s family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time.”
Arday, 41, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to his home in Battersea, south London, on Friday.
When he was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge at the age of 37 in 2023, he was the university’s youngest ever black professor.
A vigil in Arday’s memory organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism will be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday. The group’s co-convener Weyman Bennett said in a statement that Arday’s death was the “result of a racist witch-hunt”.
He added: “For more than a week, the rightwing press, politicians and the far right have hounded Jason with the most vicious racism. They are spreading the far-right lie that black people are only appointed because of the colour of our skin, rather than our ability.”
View image in fullscreen Prof Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor of Cambridge University, said her top priority was ‘supporting our community through this tragedy’. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. He denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.
When allegations surfaced in the UK media in July, Cambridge said it had investigated the claims and found no wrongdoing, describing Arday as the victim of a “vile smear campaign to undermine his credibility”.
This month, the university announced it would open a fresh investigation after it said it received “new information” about Arday’s qualifications and career.
Other elements of Arday’s life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running. He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal until the age of 11, as well as being illiterate until 18.
It is understood Cambridge has paused the investigation while Arday’s family are grieving, and will consider whether to reopen it in due course.
Academics and politicians have cast doubt on whether Cambridge took Arday’s vulnerability seriously when he was appointed to the ­senior public-facing role in 2023. At the time, the university had been facing criticism for its lack of diversity in senior roles.
Prof Simon Baron-Cohen, Arday’s friend and former colleague, told Times Radio he thought the university should proceed with the investigation. “We should see what we learn from it. This is the whole purpose of investigations,” he said.
He also questioned whether the media had failed in its duty of care towards Arday, as a vulnerable person with disabilities. He said Arday faced racist abuse and was used as a “lightning rod for a culture war on [diversity, equity and inclusion]”.
Simon Woolley, the principal of Homerton College, Cambridge, and Arday’s former mentor, has called for an investigation into the “vicious media onslaught”.
In a statement on Saturday, Prof Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor of Cambridge University, said her “thoughts and deepest condolences” were with Arday’s family, as well as with colleagues and students in the faculty of education and at Jesus College where he was a fellow.
“Supporting our community through this tragedy is the single most important priority for me and my leadership team right now. We will be reaching out to many of you directly, and we are committed to ensuring that no one feels they must face this alone,” she said.
A fundraiser launched by the Windrush campaigner Patrick Vernon on Saturday afternoon has raised more than £65,000 to contribute towards funeral and memorial costs and support for Arday’s family.
On the crowdfunder’s webpage, Vernon said: “I was one of the people who publicly supported Jason during the recent controversy because I was deeply concerned about the nature and intensity of the attacks directed towards him. I was also subject to media scrutiny for signing the letter of support and challenged in supporting Jason.”
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, described Arday’s death as a “tragedy on so many levels” and urged a “moment of reflection”.
In a statement issued via Simon & Schuster, which published Arday’s memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, in the US this week, Arday’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.
They added: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him. The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”
items.title_zh: 剑桥大学为杰森·阿尔代的心理健康支持辩护

The University of Cambridge ought to proceed with its probe into how Professor Jason Arday was recruited and his period teaching at the institution, according to a friend and former colleague.
Prof Arday, who was found dead on Friday, stepped down from his post as professor of sociology of education last week following allegations of plagiarism made against him.
Prior to his death, the university stated that it would look into the circumstances surrounding his "appointment and tenure", with the conclusions feeding into a wider review of senior recruitment processes.
It is understood that the university currently feels it would not be right to decide whether to continue the inquiry while Prof Arday’s family is grieving.
Sir Simon Baron-Cohen, a friend and former colleague of Prof Arday, told Times Radio that the university should "always be reflecting on how it’s operating and whether it can do better".
The Cambridge professor and director of the Autism Research Centre said: “They have announced an investigation, and we should let that proceed.
“We should we should see what we learn from it. This is the whole purpose of investigations.
“When you’re talking about what’s in the public interest, when you’ve got public bodies like universities or, arguably, the media, political institutions, whatever, when we have investigations, it’s all about how can we improve them.”
Sir Simon said the professor’s mental health had been left “in tatters”, adding there were questions about whether the media failed in its duty of care towards him as a vulnerable person with disabilities.
He said the professor faced racist abuse and was used as a “lightning rod for a culture war on DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion)”.
“(Prof Arday) started reporting racism within weeks of him being at Cambridge,” Sir Simon said.
“It included things like threats of physical assault to himself and his family, racist hate speech, and racist actions, hate actions.”
Lord Simon Woolley, principal of Homerton College, Cambridge, and a former mentor of Prof Arday, told BBC Radio 4’s Broadcasting House programme that his friend felt “hounded to death”.
Lord Woolley said: “In a conversation I had with Jason on the Monday – we met on Monday, with a few dear friends – he said he felt hounded to death, his words, that he couldn’t see a way out.”
He added: “On that day, we saw a man half his body weight and desperate beyond belief.”
The crossbench peer said Prof Arday had been subjected to “the most horrendous, toxic, vicious witch hunt”, and called for an investigation into the “vicious media onslaught”.
“The whole of the black community and black academics have been brought into this debate as though we don’t belong in these positions, because we are collectively the diversity, equity and inclusion hires,” Lord Woolley added.
A fundraiser for Prof Arday’s family, set up by Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon, has raised more than £60,000.
The organisation Stand Up To Racism has announced plans for a vigil for Prof Arday to be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday.
On Saturday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the professor’s death as a “tragedy on so many levels”, adding: “It’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this.”
In a statement issued by his publisher Simon & Schuster UK on Friday, Prof Arday’s family said he had been subjected to a “campaign of sustained abuse” since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge.
They said: “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”

Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Jason Arday in London in 2023. Ken McKay / ITV via Shutterstock Share Add NBC News to Google Aug. 14, 2026, 4:28 PM EDT / Updated Aug. 15, 2026, 10:45 AM EDT By Marlene Lenthang A former Cambridge professor was found dead at his London home on Friday, one week after he resigned from his position at the esteemed university following accusations of plagiarism.
Jason Arday, 41, became the youngest Black professor at Cambridge when he was hired as a professor of sociology of education in 2023.
London’s Metropolitan Police force said it responded to a report of a man found unresponsive inside a property on Friday and that the man was pronounced dead at the scene, without naming Arday. Authorities said the death is being treated as “unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.”
“We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time,” University of Cambridge Vice-Chancellor Deborah Prentice said Friday.
Arday was known for his neurodivergence; he had said he was diagnosed with autism as a child and was unable to speak until the age of 11. He went on to forge a path in academia as a scholar of race, inequality and education.
Arday had resigned on Aug. 5 following scrutiny over alleged plagiarism in his academic work and questions about his accomplishments.
Last month, questions regarding his qualifications were raised publicly by Nathan Cofnas, a former Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the institution after critiquing diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
The Times of London had subsequently published an analysis of Arday’s 2015 Ph.D. thesis highlighting passages that it said were “identical or near-identical” to an earlier paper written by another researcher.
In the weeks since, British media outlets led intense and prolonged scrutiny of Arday’s work, also interrogating a history of claims about his childhood and personal life.
A statement from Arday’s family said he was “a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone,” condemning critics who they said “would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.”
Cambridge professor Simon Baron-Cohen, director of the university’s Autism Research Centre, told the BBC he was in touch with Arday hours before his death.
He said Arday “was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life,” adding that he “wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.”
Baron-Cohen said that Arday had believed “there was a racist playbook to discredit Black academics in universities, and that they used accusations of plagiarism to try and bring down Black academics,” adding that Arday referred to former Harvard President Claudine Gay , who resigned two years ago while facing plagiarism allegations and criticism over her comments on antisemitism.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Saturday that the death was “a tragedy on so many levels,” adding that “it’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say.”

London Mayor Sadiq Khan said on X that Arday had faced “an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse” and that he “was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced.”
Hacked Off, a campaign group that supports regulation of the media, called for an “inquiry into the culture and behaviour of the British press” following the death, saying scrutiny “went far beyond any limited public interest considerations around academic standards.”
While Cambridge initially defended Arday, on Aug. 5 it opened an investigation “following new information about Professor Arday’s qualifications and honorary appointments.”
In his resignation statement last week, Arday described his tenure as “the privilege of my life to teach my students,” but conceded “the years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack.”
“While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement. The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love,” he continued.
In a statement Thursday, Cambridge’s Prentice shared an update on the inquiry into Arday, saying the university would investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the Faculty of Education in 2022 and his time at Cambridge.
She also said she asked the university council’s deputy chair and council’s audit committee to establish terms for an independent review of all university processes that will take place alongside the probe into Arday.
In his resignation announcement, Arday said he reached a point where the “personal cost becomes too great.”
“For my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away,” he said.
Arday’s memoir, “Great and Unfortunate Things,” was released earlier this week in the U.S., giving an account of his childhood — from being diagnosed with autism and developmental delays at the age of 3 — to speaking by the age of 11 and reading and writing by the age of 18.
“Without romanticizing the struggle, this is a story of determination against seemingly insurmountable odds — and of a family and a small group of believers whose compassion helped him see what is possible,” a description for the book by publisher Simon & Schuster said.

items.summary_zh: 贾森·阿尔代（Jason Arday）是一位曾任剑桥大学教授的学者，因抄袭指控而辞职。文章指出，他在辞职前遭受了无情的审视和嘲笑，感到无法承受职业和声誉的双重损失。阿尔代认为，存在一个种族主义的剧本，旨在通过抄袭指控来打击黑人学者。他的观点强调了在学术界中，针对黑人学者的抹黑行为及其对个人心理健康的严重影响。
items.l1_lead: 贾森·阿尔代因抄袭指控辞职后自杀，揭示了学术界对黑人学者的抹黑及其对心理健康的深远影响。
items.l2_summary: 贾森·阿尔代（Jason Aldine）是一位曾任剑桥大学教授的学者，近期因抄袭指控辞职，随后被发现死亡。阿尔代在辞职前经历了严厉的审视和公众的嘲笑，这使他感到难以承受职业和声誉的双重打击。他在接受采访时提到，自己认为这一切背后存在一个种族主义的剧本，旨在通过抄袭指控来打击黑人学者。他的观点揭示了在学术界中，针对黑人学者的抹黑行为不仅影响了他们的职业生涯，也对其心理健康造成了严重的负面影响。阿尔代的遭遇引发了对学术界中种族歧视问题的广泛关注，尤其是在当前社会对种族平等和公正的讨论日益增多的背景下。此事件不仅反映了个体在面对不公正指控时的脆弱，也突显了学术界在处理种族问题时的复杂性和挑战。阿尔代的死让人深思，如何在学术环境中建立一个更加包容和公正的氛围，以保护所有学者的声誉和心理健康。
